title: Two Dreams in Prison
summary: Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and chief baker are put in the prison where Joseph serves. Each has a troubling dream on the same night, and Joseph, insisting that interpretations belong to God, explains them: in three days the cupbearer will be restored and the baker executed. Both come true on Pharaoh's birthday, but the restored cupbearer forgets Joseph.
story: Joseph has gone from favored son to slave to prisoner, and chapter 39 ended with him trusted by the warden because the LORD was with him. Now the story brings two of Pharaoh's own servants into his cell. Joseph's first dreams, back in Canaan (chapter 37), got him hated and sold; here dreams return, but this time Joseph is the interpreter rather than the dreamer, and he gives the credit to God. The chapter is a hinge. It establishes that Joseph can interpret dreams truly, and it plants a man at Pharaoh's side who knows it. It also ends on a note of disappointment: Joseph asks to be remembered and is forgotten. Chapter 41 opens “two full years” later, and only then does the cupbearer's memory return.
historical:
The chapter is set in the Egyptian royal court, though, as with the rest of the Joseph story, the Pharaoh is not named and the period is debated (see the notes on chapter 39). The titles fit Egypt well. The cupbearer was a trusted official who served the king's wine and, because he was close to the king and responsible for what he drank, often had real influence; in a later century and a different empire, Nehemiah held the same post under the Persian king Artaxerxes (Nehemiah 1:11). The chief baker oversaw the preparation of the royal bread and pastries. Egyptian sources show that the palace kitchens produced a wide range of breads and cakes, which matches the “all sorts of baked goods” of verse 17.

The text doesn't say what the two officials did wrong. The word in verse 1 is simply that they “offended” or sinned against their master, and since one is restored and the other executed, the outcome presumably followed an inquiry into who was at fault.
cultural:
Egyptians took dreams seriously as messages from the gods, and specialists interpreted them. A papyrus now in the Chester Beatty collection, usually dated to the thirteenth century BC, preserves an Egyptian dream book that lists dream images and whether they mean good or bad fortune. That is why the officials are distraught: in prison they have no access to a professional interpreter, and they believe their dreams mean something important. Joseph's answer, “Don't interpretations belong to God?”, sets him apart from that system of learned technique. He claims no skill of his own.

The baker's fate would have been especially terrible to an Egyptian. Egyptian religion placed great weight on the preservation and proper burial of the body, which was thought necessary for life after death. To have one's corpse exposed and eaten by birds meant not only death but the loss of any hope beyond it. The king's birthday was an occasion for feasting and public decisions, and Egyptian texts from later centuries mention festivals held on royal birthdays.
literary: The chapter is built from matched pairs: two officials, two dreams, two interpretations, two outcomes. The dreams share a structure (three items, a royal object, the dreamer's own hands), which makes the difference between them sharper. The key is a pun on the idiom to lift up someone's head. For the cupbearer it means to restore him to honor (verse 13); for the baker, Joseph says Pharaoh “will lift off your head” (verse 19). In verse 20 the narrator uses the phrase for both men at once, “he lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker”, and then the two meanings split apart. The final verse carries the chapter's irony with a doubled statement: the cupbearer “did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.”

outline.t: Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker in prison with Joseph
Two troubling dreams, and interpretations belong to God
The cupbearer's dream and Joseph's request
Pharaoh's birthday, and the cupbearer forgets

doctrines.note: Joseph insists that the meaning of the dreams comes from God, not from human technique. The Bible treats God as the one who makes known what is hidden, a theme that returns strongly in Daniel 2.

The forgetting of verse 23 looks like the failure of Joseph's hopes. The next chapter shows that the delay placed the cupbearer's memory at exactly the moment Pharaoh would need Joseph. God's timing is often slower than human hopes, and not less wise.
Joseph names his situation honestly: he was kidnapped and has done nothing to deserve the dungeon. Faith in God's presence does not require pretending that injustice isn't injustice.

words.note: Pitron, interpretation. The noun appears in the Bible only in the Joseph story, in chapters 40 and 41. The related verb patar (H6622), to interpret, also belongs to these chapters. Joseph's point is that the interpretation of a dream is itself a gift from God, which prepares for his words to Pharaoh in 41:16.

Zakar, to remember. In the Old Testament remembering is more than recalling a fact; it means acting on behalf of someone, as when God remembered Noah (8:1) or Rachel (30:22). Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him in that full sense, and the chapter ends with the cupbearer failing to do so. Human memory fails here; God's does not.

Rosh, head. The phrase to lift up someone's head was an idiom for restoring them to favor, and it is the hinge of the chapter's wordplay: the cupbearer's head is lifted up in honor, the baker's is lifted off.

Bor, pit, cistern, or dungeon. Joseph uses it in verse 15 for the prison (the BSB's “dungeon”), and it is the same word used for the pit his brothers threw him into (37:24). His language quietly links the two injustices.

christ: Some features of this chapter have long reminded Christian readers of the gospel, and it is worth being clear that they are echoes, not predictions. A righteous man is imprisoned among two officials who have offended their king; on the third day one is restored and the other executed. At the crucifixion Jesus is placed between two condemned men, and one of them asks, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), a request Jesus grants at once. Where Joseph asks a restored man to remember him and is forgotten, Jesus is the one who remembers. More broadly, Joseph's claim that interpretation belongs to God anticipates the New Testament's claim that God has now spoken most fully in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2), the one who not only interprets God's purposes but carries them out.
questions: Joseph noticed that the two officials looked downcast and asked why, even though he himself was suffering unjustly. What would it look like to pay attention to others in the middle of your own hard season?
Joseph tells the cupbearer plainly that he has been wronged and asks for help. How do honesty about injustice and trust in God fit together?
The chapter ends with Joseph forgotten for two more years. How do you tend to respond when the help you hoped for doesn't come?
